title: The terminal state of Grove's emergency unwind is burning USDS debt, not holding recovered cash
content:
A.6.1.1.2.2.6.1.2.2.3.2 describes the goal of the recovery actions as "to recover the liquidity from Mainnet Protocols and **centralize it in the Mainnet Grove ALM Proxy**". A...3.3 then converts everything into a single unit ("centralize all recovered liquidity in USDS"), and A...3.4 ends the sequence: "repay and then burn Grove's USDS debt", via `burnUSDS(usds.balanceOf(proxy))`.

The three steps form a deliberate funnel: many positions across many protocols → one asset in one address → zero. Collapsing to a single asset first is what makes the last step expressible as one call on a balance rather than as a per-position workflow with its own decisions.

The choice to end in a burn rather than in a cash position is the substantive one. Grove's capital is minted USDS debt against Sky's allocation system, so recovered liquidity sitting idle is still an outstanding liability and still an exposure of the wider Sky balance sheet. Burning returns the system to the state it would be in if Grove had never deployed, which is the only endpoint that is unambiguously safe regardless of what the emergency turns out to be.

The implicit cost is that unwinding is not cheaply reversible: re-establishing positions afterwards requires re-minting through governance-controlled facilities and re-entering every protocol, subject to the inflow rate limits that outflows escaped.
description: The sequence ends by repaying and burning the proxy's full USDS balance, so an emergency deleverages the position rather than parking liquidity for redeployment.
